title: Municipal accommodation tax programs and lobbyist registry
subtitle: Also: social media code of conduct reviews, new water and sewer by-laws, and downtown business board appointments.
overview: Council approved an administration policy and three funding programs for the municipal accommodation tax, which is collected on hotel stays: Destination Animation, Gather Here Sponsorship and Destination Gaps and Needs. Programs start in the second quarter of 2024, and authority to award funding goes to the Deputy Chief Administrative Officer of Public Services {{vote:m9}}. Staff said applications would open in early May.

Council directed the City Clerk to draft a lobbyist registry by-law and code of conduct and report back in the third quarter of 2024 {{vote:m11}}. Council also followed a code of conduct investigation report with three separate directions: two policy reviews on personal versus corporate social media accounts, to be reported through the 2025 Governance Review, and social media training for councillors.

Through the consent report, council approved updated Water and Sewer Use by-laws, replacing versions from 1991 and 1996 {{vote:m3}}. Council also appointed two people to the Downtown Guelph Business Association board {{vote:m2}}. After the closed session, the Mayor reported that council received information and gave staff direction on a downtown land disposition. No details were released.

decisions.item: Municipal accommodation tax policy and programs
decisions.detail: Council approved the administration policy, three funding programs starting in Q2 2024, and delegated funding award authority to the Deputy Chief Administrative Officer of Public Services {{vote:m9}}.
The City Clerk will draft a Lobbyist Registry By-law and Code of Conduct and report back to Council in Q3 2024 {{vote:m11}}.

decisions.item: Code of Conduct social media review
decisions.detail: The City Clerk, with the Integrity Commissioner, will review the Code of Conduct on personal versus corporate social media accounts and report through the 2025 Governance Review {{vote:m14}}.
The Use of Corporate Resources During an Election Policy will be reviewed for social media accounts and groups, reporting back in the 2025 Governance Review {{vote:m15}}.
Staff will offer council members social media training that includes accessibility standards and guidelines {{vote:m16}}.
Council approved the updated Sewer Use By-law, replacing the 1996 by-law, as part of the consent report {{vote:m7}}.
Council approved the updated Water By-law, replacing the 1991 by-law, as part of the consent report {{vote:m8}}.
Two people were appointed to the Downtown Guelph Business Association Board of Directors for a term ending November 2026 {{vote:m2}}.

debate: A hiking trail club delegate supported the accommodation tax programs but said the examples of eligible projects were too narrow. The delegate asked that downtown beautification, such as murals, public art and facade improvements, be considered, and that the capital reserve fund support lasting tourism attractions. Staff said such items could be considered, within the annual $100,000 capital limit.

Several councillors said accommodation tax money should favour events and groups that generate overnight hotel stays, since those stays produce the revenue. One councillor asked staff to confirm that the Gather Here allocation had been increased from the original report. Staff confirmed it had.

A delegate on the lobbyist registry called it long overdue and asked for stronger consequences for violations. Staff said the draft uses escalating bans from lobbying and that monetary penalties, used only by Toronto, could be examined. Staff said non-profits would be covered where they have a financial interest, and options to broaden the definition would come back in July.

Councillors supported the registry as a transparency measure. Some said it should apply to future councils and not target individuals. One said council already recognizes delegates' interests but has had no way for them to declare it. Another asked whether the registry would be easy for community groups, and staff said it would be a couple of online forms with support.

On social media, one councillor questioned what a corporate account is, since councillors' accounts are personal, and asked why the Integrity Commissioner could not simply be consulted. The mover said the review would clarify a grey area. Staff said they would compare other Ontario municipalities. Another councillor asked that the definition cover accounts used mainly for city business. At a councillor's request, the motion was split into three parts.
